summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces, the higher-capacity digital lines used by carriers. It gives SNMP-based tools standard objects for monitoring and configuring them. It was replaced by RFC 3896.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard checklist for inspecting very big digital phone lines. Any monitoring program can ask the same questions of any maker's equipment and understand the answers.

questions: how do you monitor ds3 e3 interfaces with snmp
how does ds3 error detection work
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing high-capacity digital telecommunications lines.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to monitor and manage DS3 and E3 interfaces, which are the high-capacity digital circuits used by carriers. Different equipment vendors implement these interfaces, and operators need consistent management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a standard MIB module with SNMP objects that represent DS3 and E3 interface configuration, current status, performance statistics, and capabilities. Tools can query these objects to monitor line health, errors, and performance.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can now use SNMP to consistently monitor and configure DS3/E3 interfaces across different vendors' equipment. It was superseded by RFC 3896.

today: RFC 2496 is a Proposed Standard that defines the MIB for DS3 and E3 interface management. It was obsoleted by RFC 3896, which provides an updated and consolidated specification.

sections.title: Overview of DS3 and E3 Interfaces
sections.content:
DS3 (Digital Signal level 3) operates at 44.736 megabits per second, and E3 operates at 34.368 megabits per second; these are the backbone circuits that telephone carriers use. The RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that lets SNMP-based network management tools query and configure DS3 and E3 interfaces in a standard way.

The MIB was built to work with both SNMPv1 and SNMPv2, and it defines objects for the configuration, monitoring, and management of these high-capacity circuits. This is a successor to RFC 1407 and adds new objects for modern DS3/E3 deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Very big phone lines need checking. This document says what questions a manager program can ask any company's equipment about a big phone line, and what answers to expect.

sections.title: Configuration and Line Management
sections.content:
The configuration table lets a manager set properties of a DS3/E3 interface: the line type (which framing standard to use, such as C-bit parity or SYNTRAN), the line coding (B3ZS or HDB3), and the loopback state for diagnostics. Managers can request different types of loopbacks: line loopback, payload loopback, inward loopback, or dual loopback.

The RFC also defines support for channelization, where a single DS3 can be split into multiple DS2, DS1, or DS0 subchannels. Each channel is represented as a separate interface in the management system, and mapping tables show which channel maps to which interface.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the big phone line to do different things, like loop the signal back to test it, or split it into smaller lines. This is like adjusting knobs on the equipment.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring and Error Statistics
sections.content:
The RFC defines performance tables that collect statistics in 15-minute intervals, up to 96 intervals (24 hours of history). These include counts of line coding violations (BPV, EXZ, LCV), parity errors (PCV, CCV), errored seconds (LES, PES, CES), severely errored seconds (PSES, CSES, SEFS), and unavailable seconds (UAS).

Unavailable seconds are calculated when the line experiences 10 contiguous severely errored seconds. Once unavailable, the line is marked unavailable until 10 contiguous clean seconds occur. A rolling 24-hour total of each metric is also maintained. Agents may experience a 10-second delay in updating statistics to determine if seconds are available or unavailable, and the RFC allows for this in its requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The line gets checked every second to count errors and problems. The program remembers the last 24 hours of checking in 15-minute buckets, so you can see if things are getting worse.

sections.title: Detecting and Reporting Line Defects
sections.content:
The RFC defines several defect conditions that the interface can detect: Loss of Signal (LOS), Loss of Frame (LOF), Out of Frame (OOF), Alarm Indication Signal (AIS), and Remote Alarm Indication (RAI). A defect that persists for 2 to 10 seconds triggers a failure state; the failure clears when the defect is absent for 10 to 20 seconds.

Each defect has specific triggering conditions defined in ANSI standards (such as ANSI T1.102-1987 for DS3 and CCITT G.751 for E3). For example, LOS is declared when 175 +/- 75 contiguous pulse positions contain no pulses of either polarity. These defects are used to set the line status and, where supported, to trigger SNMP traps.
sections.plainLanguage: The line constantly checks for serious problems like complete loss of signal or the signal getting out of sync. When it detects a problem that lasts long enough to be real, it reports it.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Tables
sections.content:
The MIB is divided into groups: the Near End Group contains configuration, current statistics, 15-minute interval statistics, and 24-hour totals for the local interface. The Far End Group contains similar statistics that the remote end of the circuit sends back via the alarm/data channel.

The Fractional Table provides objects for managing sub-channels when a DS3 is channelized. The Trap Group defines alarms that the interface can send when line status changes. The RFC includes conformance information for vendors implementing different subsets of the MIB, allowing basic, intermediate, and full implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: All the checking and settings are organized into tables: one for what the local end sees, one for what the far end sends back, and others for special features like splitting the line up or sending alerts.
